content: Enterobiasis is an infection caused by the parasitic worm Enterobius vermicularis, commonly known as the pinworm. This condition primarily affects children and is characterized by symptoms such as intense itching around the anal area (perianal pruritus), restlessness, and irritability. Diagnosis is typically made through physical examination and the use of repeated scotch-tape tests, where adhesive tape is applied to the perianal skin to collect eggs for microscopic examination. Treatment involves administering two doses of antiparasitic medications such as pyrantel pamoate, albendazole, or mebendazole. Preventive measures include frequent handwashing, changing clothes regularly, and ensuring food is covered to avoid contamination. Historically, Enterobius vermicularis eggs have been identified in archaeological samples, with evidence dating back to 7837 BC in western Utah. In 1983, Jean-Pierre Hugot described a new species, Enterobius gregorii, which is morphologically identical to Enterobius vermicularis. There is no universally accepted classification system for enterobiasis, but it can be categorized based on the causative organisms, Enterobius vermicularis and Enterobius gregorii. The transmission of Enterobius vermicularis occurs via the fecal-oral route, with humans serving as the only host. The parasite reproduces in the small intestine, and gravid female worms migrate to the perianal area at night to lay eggs, causing itching. Infective eggs can also spread through contaminated dust, fomites, or fingernail contact. Enterobiasis is caused by the pinworm, a nematode (roundworm) that is a common intestinal parasite in humans. The condition is also referred to as oxyuriasis, named after the family Oxyuridae. It is important to differentiate enterobiasis from other causes of perianal itching and nematode infections. Epidemiologically, enterobiasis is particularly prevalent among children, with an estimated 200 million cases occurring annually worldwide. It is the most common parasitic worm infection in the United States and Western Europe. Risk factors include young age, poor hygiene practices, and close contact with infected individuals. Routine screening for enterobiasis is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. If left untreated, enterobiasis can lead to complications such as secondary bacterial skin infections, including bacterial dermatitis, folliculitis, vulvovaginitis, and recurrent cystitis. However, the prognosis is generally excellent with appropriate treatment. The clinical presentation of enterobiasis includes symptoms such as painful anal itching, restless sleep, poor appetite, and failure to gain weight. In severe cases, secondary bacterial infections may occur due to irritation and scratching of the anal area. On physical examination, patients may appear restless, and findings may include skin excoriations from scratching, perianal skin infections, and visible adult worms in the perianal region, particularly at night. Laboratory diagnosis is often made by observing female worms in the perianal area or using the scotch-tape test to detect eggs under a microscope. Imaging studies, such as chest X-rays, echocardiography, or ultrasound, are not relevant to the diagnosis of enterobiasis. Treatment involves the use of antiparasitic drugs such as mebendazole, albendazole, piperazine, or pyrantel pamoate. A second dose is recommended two weeks after the initial treatment to ensure eradication. Since multiple household members are often infected, treating the entire household is advised. Surgical intervention is not indicated for enterobiasis. Primary prevention strategies include treating all family members, frequent handwashing, and improving personal and household hygiene. Secondary prevention measures are identical to primary prevention strategies.
